questions.question: Explain how designers find out what a society needs before building a technology, and why the needs of a city suburb and a rural village may lead to different tower designs.
questions.expected_answer: Designers gather needs from the people who have them: surveys and interviews, public meetings, studying how existing technology is used and where it fails, data such as failed emergency calls, and consultation with local leaders, municipalities and services. The ranked needs become the design brief. A city suburb needs high capacity for many users and objects to visual pollution, so it gets a short, disguised or monopole tower on mains power; a rural village needs wide basic coverage for calls and mobile money with no reliable electricity, so it gets a tall bare tower on solar panels and batteries.

questions.question: List three positive and three negative impacts of a cell phone tower on a community, and explain what is meant by saying impacts fall unevenly.
questions.expected_answer: Positive: the clinic can call an ambulance quickly, schools gain internet access, families receive money by phone, shops take card payments, farmers check prices, people receive flood warnings. Negative: the mast spoils views and is lit at night, residents fear health effects, screen time affects sleep and schoolwork, scams spread, some jobs disappear, battery theft cuts coverage. Impacts fall unevenly because people within range benefit while those just beyond do not, and people who cannot afford phones or data fall further behind as services move online, the digital divide.

questions.question: Describe the environmental impacts of a cell phone tower over its whole life and give three design responses that reduce them.
questions.expected_answer: Before construction: mining and smelting steel and making concrete release carbon dioxide, and roads and transport disturb soil and plants. During use: constant electricity consumption, diesel generators burning fuel and making noise and fumes, night lights disorientating insects and birds, and guy wires killing birds. At end of life: steel is recyclable but batteries containing lead or lithium and old electronics are hazardous waste. Responses: site on existing roads and disturbed ground, share towers between networks, use solar panels and batteries instead of diesel, shield lights and mark guy wires, choose recyclable materials and plan for removal.
